habitat: Arabian leopards are the smallest and most critically endangered leopard subspecies, surviving only in fragmented pockets of the Arabian Peninsula — primarily in the Dhofar Mountains of Oman, the Hajjah region of Yemen, and possibly the Negev Desert of Israel. They inhabit arid mountain ranges, rocky escarpments, and wadis (dry river valleys) with sparse vegetation including acacia trees and drought-resistant shrubs. They require rocky outcrops for denning and vantage points for hunting. With fewer than 200 individuals remaining, they are one of the rarest big cats on Earth.
diet: Arabian leopards prey on the limited fauna of the Arabian Peninsula, including Nubian ibex, Arabian gazelle, rock hyrax, hares, foxes, birds, and occasionally domestic livestock. Due to scarce wild prey populations from overhunting, these leopards increasingly target goats, sheep, and camels, bringing them into lethal conflict with herders. They are ambush hunters, using rocky terrain and sparse cover to stalk within striking distance. A large kill may sustain a leopard for a week or more.
behavior: Arabian leopards are solitary and territorial, with males maintaining larger ranges that overlap those of females. They are primarily nocturnal to avoid the extreme desert heat, resting in caves, rock crevices, and shaded overhangs during the day. They require enormous territories of 100-350 square kilometers due to low prey density. Females give birth to 1-2 cubs, which remain dependent for 12-18 months. Their vocalizations include sawing calls (territorial advertisement), chuffing (friendly greeting), and growls (warning). They can survive for extended periods without drinking, obtaining moisture from their prey.
facts: The Arabian leopard is the smallest leopard subspecies, with males weighing approximately 30 kg and females 20 kg. Their coat is pale, almost tawny-yellow, reflecting their desert environment—rosettes are widely spaced on a light background. They are genetically distinct, having separated from African leopards approximately 500,000 years ago. The subspecies was declared extinct in the wild in Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Oman's captive breeding program at the Arabian Leopard Breeding Centre is crucial for survival. Fewer than 200 survive today.
naming: Arabian leopard names might reflect their desert home or Arabian Peninsula origin. Consider names like Sahara, Dune, Oman, Mirage, Sirocco (desert wind), Wadi, Layth (lion in Arabic — symbolic for strength), Najm (star in Arabic), Zafir (victorious), or Qamar (moon in Arabic).
